Memory Systems

You can hold a new phone number in your head for a few seconds, describe your last vacation, and ride a bike you haven’t touched in years. Are these all the same kind of memory? This lesson maps the memory systems that support movement.

Working vs. long-term memory Knowing how vs. knowing that Three hands-on demos

By the end of this lesson

Learning objectives

You should be able to:

  • 1Compare working memory and long-term memory (duration, capacity, processing) and explain how chunking stretches working memory.
  • 2Distinguish procedural, episodic, and semantic memory, and declarative vs. procedural knowledge.
  • 3Use the case of patient H.M. to explain why “knowing how” and “knowing that” rely on partly separate systems.
  • 4Give examples of explicit and implicit memory tests.
  • 5Link brain memory systems to clinical patterns in Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease.
Getting started

What is memory?

“The capacity that permits organisms to benefit from past experiences”
Endel Tulving (1985), University of Toronto

Notice how close this is to our definition of learning. Everything we covered about learning this semester (practice schedules, feedback, retention tests) comes down to one question: does today’s practice still change performance tomorrow? That’s memory.

Memory isn’t one thing. Here is the map we’ll work through in this lesson:

Tulving, E. (1985). How many memory systems are there? American Psychologist, 40(4), 385–398. doi:10.1037/0003-066X.40.4.385 · Squire, L. R. (2004). Memory systems of the brain: A brief history and current perspective. Neurobiology of Learning and Memory, 82(3), 171–177. doi:10.1016/j.nlm.2004.06.005

What just happened?

Working memory is small, and chunking stretches it

Your Copy me! scores will appear here.

Most people do well at 3 and 5 moves and start losing track somewhere around 5–7 moves. That’s the limit of working memory, the small, short-lived store you used to hold the sequence until you could reproduce it.

7 ± 2
items: the classic estimate of working memory span (Miller, 1956)
~4
chunks: a newer estimate once people can’t rehearse or group items (Cowan, 2001)

A chunk is a meaningful unit. When three moves are named as one phrase (“The Wake-Up”), nine moves fit into three “slots” instead of nine. That’s why Round 5 usually goes better than Round 4, even though both have nine moves. It’s also how dancers learn choreography: in counts and named phrases (“5, 6, 7, 8”), not single steps.

In the clinic

Chunking works for patients too. Teach a home exercise program as two or three named routines rather than ten separate exercises (PT); break dressing into short named phrases such as “arm in, over the head, pull down” (OT); or group an instrument setup into a familiar sequence you always run in the same order (dentistry).

Miller, G. A. (1956). The magical number seven, plus or minus two. Psychological Review, 63(2), 81–97. doi:10.1037/h0043158 · Cowan, N. (2001). The magical number 4 in short-term memory. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 24(1), 87–114. doi:10.1017/S0140525X01003922

Predict · expert dancers

Do experts have bigger memories, or bigger chunks?

Starkes and colleagues (1987) tested young ballet dancers on exactly the kind of task you just did.

Dancers11-year-olds: 8 experts · 8 novices
Sequences8 ballet steps, either choreographed or randomly ordered
RecallPerform the steps back

Make two predictions, then flip each card.

The take-away

Expertise doesn’t seem to enlarge working memory itself. Instead, it builds bigger chunks drawn from long-term memory. Chess masters show the same pattern: they remember real game positions far better than novices, but the advantage shrinks for randomly placed pieces (Chase & Simon, 1973).

Clinical version: an experienced clinician sees a gait pattern as one unit (“that’s a Trendelenburg gait”), where a student still sees separate joint deviations.

Starkes, J. L., Deakin, J. M., Lindley, S., & Crisp, F. (1987). Motor versus verbal recall of ballet sequences by young expert dancers. Journal of Sport Psychology, 9(3), 222–230. doi:10.1123/jsp.9.3.222 · Chase, W. G., & Simon, H. A. (1973). Perception in chess. Cognitive Psychology, 4(1), 55–81. doi:10.1016/0010-0285(73)90004-2

Two stores

Working memory vs. long-term memory

Baddeley’s model describes working memory as a mental “workbench” where you hold, compare, and use information right now. Long-term memory is the warehouse. For each row, predict how the two differ, then click a cell to check.

Working memoryLong-term memory
Duration revealAbout 20–30 seconds without rehearsal revealRelatively permanent
Capacity revealLimited: 7 ± 2 items, or about 4 chunks revealPractically unlimited
Processing revealRehearse, compare, decide, solve problems revealEncode, store, and retrieve
Motor example revealHolding your therapist’s cue in mind while you plan the next attempt, or comparing feedback from your last try with what you intended revealKnowing how to swim, drive, or tie a surgical knot

Baddeley, A. D., & Hitch, G. (1974). Working memory. Psychology of Learning and Motivation, 8, 47–89. doi:10.1016/S0079-7421(08)60452-1 · Baddeley, A. (2012). Working memory: Theories, models, and controversies. Annual Review of Psychology, 63, 1–29. doi:10.1146/annurev-psych-120710-100422 · Smyth, M. M., & Pendleton, L. R. (1989). Working memory for movements. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology A, 41(2), 235–250. doi:10.1080/14640748908402363

Inside long-term memory

Three kinds of long-term memory

A tennis player remembers three very different things. For each card, decide which kind of memory it is, then flip.

Declarative knowledgeEpisodic + semantic. You can say it.
Procedural knowledgeYou show it by doing it.

Squire, L. R. (2004). doi:10.1016/j.nlm.2004.06.005 · Tulving, E. (1985). doi:10.1037/0003-066X.40.4.385

Sort it

Procedural, episodic, or semantic?

Classify each memory. Wrong picks turn red; keep trying until each one is right.

0 / 6 sorted
A dental student remembers the morning she gave her very first local anesthetic injection.
✓ Episodic: a personal event tied to a time and place.
An OT knows that a stroke on the right side of the brain usually weakens the left side of the body.
✓ Semantic: a general fact, not tied to when she learned it.
A PT smoothly guides a patient through a bed-to-wheelchair transfer without thinking through each step.
✓ Procedural: a skill shown by doing it.
Knowing that the ACL keeps the tibia from sliding forward on the femur.
✓ Semantic: textbook knowledge you can state.
Riding a bicycle again after ten years without one.
✓ Procedural: well-learned skills are remarkably durable (more on this in Lesson 2).
Remembering the crowd noise and the final score of last season’s championship game you played in.
✓ Episodic: your own experience of a specific event.
A famous case

Patient H.M.: knowing how without knowing that

In 1953, Henry Molaison (known for decades as “H.M.”) had surgery for severe epilepsy that removed the medial temporal lobe on both sides, including much of the hippocampus. Watch the short clip, then predict what happened when he practiced a new motor skill.

Video not loading? Open it on YouTube
LostThe ability to form new declarative memories (anterograde amnesia). He couldn’t remember people he met or events after the surgery.
SparedWorking memory, intelligence, language, and most memories from before the surgery. He could hold information for a few seconds, but it didn’t transfer into long-term memory.
Two take-aways

1. “Knowing how” and “knowing that” rely on partly separate memory systems.

2. Forming new declarative memories depends on the hippocampus and medial temporal lobe, while motor skill learning can proceed without them.

A small correction to the textbook story

When H.M.’s brain was examined after his death, more of the back of the hippocampus remained than had been believed, and there was a small additional lesion in the frontal lobe (Annese et al., 2014). “Hippocampus removed” is a useful simplification.

Corkin, S. (1968). Acquisition of motor skill after bilateral medial temporal-lobe excision. Neuropsychologia, 6(3), 255–265. doi:10.1016/0028-3932(68)90024-9 · Corkin, S. (2002). What’s new with the amnesic patient H.M.? Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 3(2), 153–160. doi:10.1038/nrn726 · Annese, J., et al. (2014). Postmortem examination of patient H.M.’s brain based on histological sectioning and digital 3D reconstruction. Nature Communications, 5, 3122. doi:10.1038/ncomms4122

How do we know someone remembers?

Explicit vs. implicit memory tests

H.M. would have failed a test that asked him to remember practicing, yet passed one that measured his tracing. The kind of test matters.

Explicit testsAsk you to consciously remember.
Recall: “Describe the steps of your transfer.” “Show me the arm position from earlier.”
Recognition: “Which of these three videos shows the routine you learned?”
Implicit testsShow learning through performance, even if you can’t say what you learned.
Getting faster on a repeating sequence than on a random one; H.M.’s mirror drawing.
Clinical point

A patient who “fails” an explicit test may still be learning. If someone can’t describe last week’s exercise but performs it better, the practice is working. Check performance, not just what they can tell you.

Next, let’s run the classic implicit test on you.

Knowledge check
Mr. Lopez has early Alzheimer’s disease. He practices making a cup of coffee in the clinic kitchen with his OT three times a week. Each session he says he has never done this before, yet he makes the coffee more smoothly and with fewer mistakes week after week. What does this pattern show?
What you can now do

Summary & the next step

  • 1Working memory is brief and small (about 7 ± 2 items, or about 4 chunks). Chunking, and the bigger chunks that come with expertise, stretch it.
  • 2Long-term memory includes procedural memory (knowing how) and declarative memory (knowing that), which splits into episodic and semantic.
  • 3H.M. showed that forming new declarative memories depends on the hippocampus, while motor skills can still be learned without it.
  • 4Explicit tests ask people to recall or recognize; implicit tests reveal learning through performance (mirror drawing, the serial reaction time task).
  • 5Separate brain systems mean different clinical strategies: more doing in Alzheimer’s, explicit cues in Parkinson’s.
